task.title: Phone app that works on its own, with no computer running Workbook
task.description:
Workbook reaches a phone today only by pointing its browser at a `workbook serve` running on some computer, so the board is gone the moment that computer sleeps or leaves the network. This story is a phone app that needs no computer at all: it holds its own copy of a project's tasks, talks to the project's Git remote itself, and keeps working with no signal.

The use case is the time away from the desk: check what is next, read a task, capture an idea as a new task, move something along, and have teammates and agents see that change the next time they sync.

## What "no computer" means

- The app is given a project's remote URL and credentials, fetches `refs/workbook/tasks/*` from it, and builds its own projection on the device. No `workbook serve`, desktop app, relay, or hosted Workbook service sits in between; the only other party is the Git host the team already uses.
- A change made on the phone is an ordinary Workbook operation commit, written in the same versioned format the CLI writes, and pushed to the single task ref it changed. A CLI or desktop user cannot tell which client made it except by attribution.
- With no connection the app still opens, reads, and accepts edits. Those edits are shown as not yet published until the remote accepts them, and publish on their own when the connection returns.
- The existing rules hold unchanged: task history is append-only and never force-pushed, a rejected push is refetched and reapplied rather than overwritten, concurrent edits to the same field surface as a conflict instead of one side vanishing, and the on-device projection can be thrown away and rebuilt from the refs.

## What makes this more than a new front end

- A phone has no `git` binary, and `internal/gitstore` reaches Git by running one. The phone needs another way to fetch, write objects, and push, behind the same narrow repository interface, and it must not assume a hash algorithm.
- The projection is already portable: SQLite comes from `modernc.org/sqlite`, which is pure Go.
- A code repository can be large. The app wants the task refs only, never the project's source tree or branches.
- Credentials for the remote live on the phone, so they need the platform's secure storage and a sign-in a person can complete with their thumbs.
- Derived facts that depend on code history, such as branch inclusion and landed state, may be unavailable without the code. The app says so rather than showing a wrong answer.

## Decisions to settle before building

Settle these first and record the outcome on this task; each one that turns into real work becomes its own task depending on this one.

1. Platform: iPhone, Android, or both, and which comes first.
2. How the Workbook core gets onto the phone: compile the existing Go core for mobile with a Git implementation that needs no binary, or reimplement operation writing and projection in the platform's language. Reuse keeps one implementation of the conflict rules; a spike has to show it is actually workable before it is chosen.
3. Screens: native screens, or the existing web board shown inside the app against an in-app server. The board was not designed for a phone-sized screen either way.
4. Sign-in: which remotes and credential types the first version supports (HTTPS with a token, a host's device sign-in flow, SSH keys).
5. First-version scope. Proposed: several projects, the board and Next views, task detail, create, edit title, description, status, priority and labels, and assign to self. Proposed out: project setup, status and priority vocabulary changes, conflict resolution beyond showing that one exists, and anything destructive.
6. Distribution: store listing or a test channel first, and where its release sits beside the CLI and desktop release lines.

"Create an app bundle to deploy the web server" is the other way to put Workbook on a phone, through a hosted board. It is a different product decision with a service to run, and this story does not depend on it.

## Done when

- With every computer that has the project switched off and the phone on cellular data, a person adds a project by its remote URL, sees its board, creates a task and changes another's status, and a teammate's next `workbook list` shows both.
- In airplane mode the app opens, shows the last known board, accepts an edit, marks it unpublished, and publishes it without help after the connection returns.
- An edit made on the phone and a different edit to the same field made from the CLI while the phone was offline both survive as a visible conflict.
- Deleting the app's local data and adding the project again reproduces the same board from the remote.
- The README and `docs/architecture.md` describe the phone as a second client of the same refs, with what is guaranteed and what is best effort when offline stated separately.
